None of this is compulsory. All of it will make the first morning easier.

## The workshop introduction deck

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
[**Modern Research & Data Science: Philosophy, Paradigms, and AI-Augmented Reproducibility**](../slides/workshop_intro.html){target="_blank"}
:::

Four parts: philosophy of knowledge (ontology, epistemology, induction and
deduction); the frequentist, Bayesian and AI paradigms; methodological
applications in clinical research; and the modern AI-augmented stack of R,
Quarto and generative AI.

Skim it. The argument that matters for these two days is the last one: that
your choice of tools is downstream of a philosophical position about what
counts as knowledge, and that reproducibility is where that position becomes
checkable by other people.

## Why reproducibility, specifically

Three short pieces, in increasing order of discomfort:

1. **Peng RD.** [Reproducible research in computational science](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1213847).
   *Science* 2011;334:1226–7. Two pages. Introduces the reproducibility
   spectrum — from "publication only" to "full replication" — that we use to
   frame Session 1.

2. **Baker M.** [1,500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility](https://doi.org/10.1038/533452a).
   *Nature* 2016;533:452–4. The survey where most researchers reported
   failing to reproduce someone else's experiment — and more than half failed
   to reproduce their own.

3. **Ziemann M, Eren Y, El-Osta A.** [Gene name errors are widespread in the scientific literature](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-1044-7).
   *Genome Biology* 2016;17:177. About a fifth of genomics papers with Excel
   supplementary files contained gene names silently converted to dates. The
   most quietly devastating paper on this list, and the best argument for a
   scripted workflow you will ever read.

## On teaching and learning with data

- **Cook DA, Beckman TJ.** [Current concepts in validity and reliability for psychometric instruments](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2005.10.036).
  *Am J Med* 2006;119:166.e7–16. Relevant if you plan to bring your own
  assessment data to the group activity.

- **Wickham H.** [Tidy data](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10).
  *Journal of Statistical Software* 2014;59(10). The one-sentence version:
  each variable a column, each observation a row, each type of observational
  unit a table. Everything `dplyr` does on Day 1 afternoon assumes it.

## On generative AI in research

Read at least one of these before Day 2 afternoon:

- **ICMJE.** [Recommendations: use of AI-assisted technology](https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/).
  The rule that matters: AI tools cannot be authors, and their use must be
  disclosed.

- **WHO.** [Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: guidance on large multi-modal models](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240084759).
  2024. Skim the governance section.

- **NITI Aayog.** [National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence](https://www.niti.gov.in/national-strategy-artificial-intelligence).
  Context for the "AI ecosystem in India" part of Session 8.

## Books, if you catch the bug

| | |
|---|---|
| [R for Data Science (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) | Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund. Free online. The default answer to "what should I read next?" |
| [The Epidemiologist R Handbook](https://epirhandbook.com/) | Task-oriented, health-specific, and free. Excellent for looking things up |
| [Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/) | Genuinely good official docs, which is rare |
| [Telling Stories with Data](https://tellingstorieswithdata.com/) | Alexander. Free online. Strong on the workflow and ethics side |

## A note on how to read all this

You are not expected to absorb it. Skim now, and come back after the
workshop when the words have referents. The single most useful thing you can
do before 9 September is finish [the R primer](r-primer.qmd) — a concept you
have typed once beats a concept you have read three times.
